functional_compartments.name: Single fiber population

neuromuscular_junction_zone.location_description: mid-belly endplate band -- for where this band lies along the muscle, see motor_endplate_zones

functional_compartments.function_note: Absent unilaterally or bilaterally in roughly 10-15% of people (population variation, not a defect) -- the standard textbook example of a functionally dispensable muscle, commonly harvested as a tendon graft when present.
functional_compartments.source: Holzbaur KR, Murray WM, Delp SL (2005) Ann Biomed Eng 33(6):829-840 -- upper-extremity muscle architecture model (fascicle length, pennation, PCSA)

motor_endplate_zones.method: modified Sihler's stain intramuscular nerve-dense region, with muscle-spindle abundance histology
motor_endplate_zones.notes: Nerve-dense region of about 3.17 cm2. Highest spindle abundance in its upper third, at 31.77% of muscle length. Palmaris longus had the lowest spindle abundance of the eight muscles studied, and is absent altogether in a substantial minority of people.
motor_endplate_zones.source: Zhou J, Jia F, Chen P, Zhou G, Wang M, Wu J, Yang S, 'Localisation of the centre of the highest region of muscle spindle abundance of anterior forearm muscles', J Anat 244(5):803-814 (2023), doi:10.1111/joa.14000 -- 24 adult cadavers, modified Sihler's staining with muscle-spindle histology and spiral CT localisation

trigger_points.location_description: Mid-belly, on the line from the medial epicondyle to the middle of the wrist crease, near the junction of the proximal and middle thirds of the forearm.
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Superficial, needle-like or prickling pain in the palm (distal palm and bases of the fingers), with spillover to the distal volar forearm; patients report a tender palm and difficulty handling tools.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Prolonged gripping of narrow tools, falls onto the palm, direct palmar trauma; associated trigger points in flexor carpi radialis, flexor carpi ulnaris, pronator teres and the finger flexors.
trigger_points.notes: Travell and Simons report that palmaris longus trigger points frequently accompany Dupuytren's contracture and palmar pain, and that inactivating them relieves the pain component without changing the contracture. Non-myofascial differential: Dupuytren's disease, palmar fasciitis, carpal tunnel syndrome, ulnar tunnel syndrome, hypothenar hammer syndrome.
trigger_points.source: Simons, Travell & Simons (1999) Trigger Point Manual, 2nd ed., Vol. 1, ch. 37; Donnelly et al. (2019) 3rd ed., ch. 37, pp. 360-365 -- as cited in this atlas's uploaded wrist muscle reference.

clinical.compiled_by: repository owner (physician); elbow_muscles_reference_v2.html, compiled 04/09/2026 (v2; v1 31/08/2026). Strength data come from the Mayo elbow series (An et al. 1981; Askew et al. 1987), from MRI/cadaver architecture studies (Murray et al. 2000; Kawakami et al. 1994) and from Neumann (2017). Values are population means; individual variation is large.
clinical.function_biomechanics: Palmaris longus tenses the palmar aponeurosis, cupping the palm and anchoring the palmar skin during grip; it is a weak wrist flexor and its elbow moment is negligible. Its absence produces no measurable deficit in grip or pinch, which is why it is the standard tendon graft and tendon-transfer donor.
clinical.adjacent_structures: Adjacent bursae: None. Adjacent structures and relations: The median nerve lies deep and slightly radial to the tendon at the wrist (between PL and FCR); the palmar cutaneous branch runs along its radial side; the ulnar neurovascular bundle lies medial under FCU. The tendon is the classic landmark for carpal tunnel injection (ulnar to it).

trigger_points.location: Mid-belly in the proximal half of the forearm, medial to FCR; the muscle is identified by opposing thumb to little finger with the wrist flexed.
trigger_points.referred_pain: a superficial prickling, needle-like pain in the palm, concentrated in the distal palm and the base of the thumb, sometimes extending to the distal anterior forearm.
trigger_points.notes: Symptoms / mimics: Palm tenderness and soreness when handling tools; Travell & Simons noted the association with Dupuytren's contracture and recommended treating PL TrPs in that setting. Entrapment: None. Associated TrPs: FCR, FCU, finger flexors, pronator teres.
trigger_points.source: Travell & Simons, vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1999: ch. 37, Palmaris longus.

pain_referred_into_this_muscle_from: latissimus dorsi and pectoralis muscles (ulnar palm)
clinical.pain_referred_into_territory: Pain referred INTO this territory (palm) from elsewhere
clinical.notes: Confirm presence (Schaeffer's test) before planning a graft; local agenesis rates are high. A variant PL (reversed, bifid, accessory) can compress the median or ulnar nerve at the wrist.
clinical.caveat: Clinical reference for professional use; anatomical variation is frequent and trigger-point patterns describe typical, not universal, presentations. Referred pain is presented in both directions: pain that each muscle's TrPs refer to other regions, and pain that other muscles (shoulder, chest, back) and non-muscular sources refer into the elbow region. Where Travell & Simons did not map a muscle separately (extensor digiti minimi, pronator quadratus) this is stated rather than filled in.
sources: Travell & Simons, vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1999: ch. 37, Palmaris longus.
Yammine K. Clinical prevalence of palmaris longus agenesis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Clin Anat 2013;26(6):709–718.

(2019) for trigger-point (TrP) locations and referred-pain patterns; Green's Operative Hand Surgery 8th ed. (2022) [4], Neumann (2017) [5], Kendall (2005) [6] and Kapandji (2019) [7] for kinesiology, Netter (2023) [54] for topographic cross-checking; and peer-reviewed primary literature for biomechanics, variants and clinical entities. Bracketed numbers point to the master list in Appendix B; every profile ends with its own reference list. Claims that could not be tied to a verified source are labelled [clinical reasoning] or [UNVERIFIED]. Appendix A grades the match between each key claim and its source.
clinical.function_biomechanics: Major: Tensions the palmar aponeurosis, anchoring palmar skin during grip and assisting cupping of the palm [1, 5]. Minor: Weak wrist flexion; minor thumb abduction through thenar slips [1, 6]. Small tension fraction relative to the other flexors [13]. Importance: Functionally expendable: agenesis causes no measurable grip deficit [grade C]; the preferred free tendon graft (pulley and flexor reconstructions, ligament reconstructions) and a transfer donor (Camitz opponensplasty, PL to EPL) [4].
clinical.adjacent_structures: Bursae / sheaths: None. The tendon lies in the antebrachial fascia superficial to the palmar carpal ligament. Coupled structures: Palmar aponeurosis and Dupuytren's tissue; median nerve and its palmar cutaneous branch; the tendon is the standard surface landmark for the median nerve at the wrist [1, 4].

trigger_points.location: Mid-belly, on the line from the medial epicondyle to the middle of the wrist crease, near the junction of the proximal and middle thirds of the forearm [2, 3].
trigger_points.referred_pain: Superficial, needle-like or prickling pain in the palm (distal palm and bases of the fingers), with spillover to the distal volar forearm; patients report a tender palm and difficulty handling tools ("Variant Vandal", chapter 37) [2, 3].
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Prolonged gripping of narrow tools, falls onto the palm, direct palmar trauma; associated TrPs in FCR, FCU, PT and the finger flexors [2, 3].

pain_referred_into_this_muscle_from: Pectoralis major and minor (palm and ulnar digits)
clinical.non_myofascial_differential: Dupuytren's disease, palmar fasciitis, carpal tunnel syndrome, ulnar tunnel syndrome, hypothenar hammer syndrome.
clinical.notes: Surgical relevance is chiefly as a donor and as a landmark. Median-nerve compression by a reversed PL is a recognized variant cause of carpal-tunnel-like symptoms. Travell and Simons report that PL trigger points frequently accompany Dupuytren's contracture and palmar pain, and that inactivating them relieves the pain component without changing the contracture [2, 3].
clinical.caveat: Referred-pain maps from Travell and Simons are clinical consensus drawings, not experimentally derived; the APL and pronator quadratus maps (Hwang et al.) are experimental hypertonic-saline studies in healthy volunteers. Grade C items (Appendix A rows 23, 44–46, 48): TrP distances, muscle-level arterial detail, the ECRL/ECRB insertional bursa, the grip-strength claim for PL agenesis, and the extrapolated EDM/EPB/EPL referral statements. All are labelled in the text. Referred-pain conventions. "TrP referral" is the essential (dark) zone described by Travell and Simons unless "spillover" is stated. TrP locations in centimetres are approximations read from the Manual's figures and should be confirmed by palpation of the taut band. Quantitative biomechanical values are cadaveric means and vary with forearm rotation and wrist angle.
